payload.title: What Are the Nigerian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
protect_keywords: 10 nigerian wedding customs (old URL; SEO to quantify US and AU)
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, one or both of Nigerian heritage (Yoruba, Igbo or Hausa-Fulani) or marrying into a Nigerian family, who want to understand what each family will expect (introduction and engagement, bride price and the list, iku aka and igba nkwu, nikah and kamu, aso ebi, spraying, the white wedding) and plan how to hold these customs at a wedding in Australia or at a destination elsewhere, since Smartraveller currently advises Australians to reconsider travel to Nigeria.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed after the 'bringing the customs home' section.
payload.angle: Most lists treat 'Nigerian' as one wedding and lean on party clichés. We separate the three largest traditions as families live them: the Yoruba introduction and engagement with prostrating greetings, gele, fila and aso oke; the Igbo iku aka, the bride price list and igba nkwu; the Hausa-Fulani nikah and kamu; then what all share, aso ebi, spraying and the white wedding held alongside the traditional one. Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups, so we say once that customs vary by family, group and faith. Because Smartraveller advises Australians to reconsider travel to Nigeria, we close with how Nigerian-Australian and mixed-heritage couples bring these customs to a wedding in Australia or at a destination elsewhere: fabric lead times, two-ceremony timing, music, and space for spraying and dancing.
must_include: One early framing line: Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups and customs differ between Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa-Fulani families and by faith

About 11 numbered customs grouped by people: Yoruba (introduction and idana, prostrating and kneeling, gele fila and aso oke), Hausa-Fulani (nikah and sadaki, kamu), Igbo (iku aka, bride price and list, igba nkwu), shared (aso ebi, spraying, the white wedding)
Each custom tied to its group only where a source does; faith only where sourced; terms with tone marks as sources give them; inline definitions
Bride price, gift lists, sadaki and spraying with no amounts

Section for Australians: Smartraveller 'Reconsider your need to travel' overall and 'Do not travel' areas, dated once 'as at November 2026'; no suggestion to marry in Nigeria; Australian High Commission Abuja; any legal line as a question
Diaspora planning section: aso ebi ordering and lead times, timing traditional and white weddings, music, MC or alaga, space and run sheet for spraying and dancing, 'ask your celebrant'
FAQ of 5 to 7 questions with no amounts, covering old-page queries (two weddings, money spraying, matching outfits, bride price)

Internal links: /destinations/africa, /expert-advice/african-honeymoons-private-safari-and-island-escapes-by-season, /wonderland-studio/wedding-website-templates/african (priority), related traditions drafts, /expert-advice/wedding-traditions pillar

tradition_plan.note: Planner (wedding-planner-sme) runs batch A and batch B in parallel, scratch folders 02-research/batch-a and 02-research/batch-b, 15 min HARD by the clock, save after every 3 facts, no extra sourcing rounds, never retry a declined call. Preferred sources: National Council for Arts and Culture and other Nigerian government culture pages, British Museum, Smithsonian NMAfA, V&A (aso oke), UNESCO, Britannica, academic sources. Never competitor wedding sites, vendor blogs or Wikipedia. Unsourced customs are written as living practice ('In many Yoruba families...') with no meaning or origin as fact and no [[VERIFY]] marker; 'often told' at most once per post. Source gaps go in the run report only (authority rule). Nothing on harmful or contested practices.
